https://www.baltictimes.com/housing_as_a.text: Estonia Latvia Lithuania Business Analysis Opinions Culture EU Affairs Search Archive Housing as an economic and security issue: European Parliament delegation led by Inese Vaidere arrives in Riga 2026-07-20 EPP group Today, 20 July, a European Parliament delegation led by Inese Vaidere MEP arrives in Riga to assess housing policy and housing affordability in Latvia, housing finance, as well as regional and security challenges in this area. The delegation of the European Parliament’s Special Committee on the Housing Crisis (HOUS) also includes Members from France, Austria and Croatia. “Housing is not only the foundation of a family. It is a prerequisite for economic development and, increasingly, also a matter of security. If Latvia’s regions and eastern border areas continue to lose population and if families cannot afford housing there, this will, in the long term, affect the development and security of the entire country and the European Union ,” emphasised Inese Vaidere MEP (EPP Group), member of the EP committee. “While in Southern Europe, short-term rental housing is putting pressure on the long-term rental market, and in Central Europe it is a housing shortage, the challenges in the Baltic states are different, including residential buildings constructed during the Soviet occupation that do not meet quality standards. People are particularly concerned about the high cost of rental apartments and the fact that it is difficult for young people to buy their first home - bank requirements are too high. For seniors and families, heating bills in uninsulated buildings are a heavy burden, while regions often lack funding. These problems require an urgent solution at the national level ,” the Inese Vaidere noted. “Although housing policy falls within the competence of each EU member state, at European level we help coordinate and identify best practices, conduct research and develop proposals for the necessary regulatory framework. Bureaucracy must be reduced by reviewing regulations that directly affect the housing sector,” explained Vaidere, who is the only Latvian Member serving on this committee. “I invited my colleagues from the European Parliament to brief them with the situation in Latvia. We face challenges that must be addressed, but we also have examples from which other countries can learn, such as the digitalisation of certain processes. The interests and challenges of our region must certainly be taken into account, as we are located at the external border of the EU,” she added. The visit to Riga is scheduled for two days, 20 - 21 July. During the visit, meetings are planned with representatives of the Riga City Council and the Ministry of Economics, the state development finance institution “Altum”, the Riga Energy Agency, as well as NGO’s and several sector experts. Following this, the MEPs, led by Inese Vaidere (EPP Group), will travel to Finland for a two-day visit. Comments Related Articles Subscribe Log In Ads Please enter your username and password. Photograph: Amer Ghazzal/Alamy View image in fullscreen Pupils demonstrating in Parliament Square, London, demanding urgent action to tackle climate change in 2019. Photograph: Amer Ghazzal/Alamy Education Letters British students, like their French peers, have been known to challenge authority Pete Crockett says the history of British education is not simply one of children dutifully accepting adult instruction, while Simon Dawson says Kitty Sayers misses the mark when describing English attitudes. Plus a letter from Kevin Donnelly Fri 16 Oct 2026 12.32 EDT Last modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 12.34 EDT Share Reading Kitty Sayers’ interesting article, I was reminded of the rich, and perhaps too easily forgotten, history of direct action by British schoolchildren ( Angry French students take to the streets. British students don’t – and I think I know why, 10 October ). Far from being historically meek or unquestioningly compliant, they have demonstrated a remarkable capacity for challenging authority. At Marlborough college, troops were once summoned to dislodge rebellious pupils occupying an island in the school grounds. In the late 1700s , Winchester college experienced several rebellions. Nor was such defiance confined to the more privileged. In 1889 , strikes by schoolchildren in the Scottish lowlands spread across Tyneside, London, Bristol and Cardiff. In 1911 , a strike beginning at Bigyn school in Llanelli developed into a remarkable wave of protest, reaching some 60 towns across England and Wales. Schoolchildren and their families also played their part in the extraordinary 1914 Burston school strike , which endured for 25 years and became the longest‑running strike in British history. Those of us of a certain generation may also recall the National Union of School Students in the 1970s, whose challenges to established educational authority infuriated traditionalists such as the headmaster Rhodes Boyson , who later became a Conservative minister. The history of British education is not simply one of children dutifully accepting adult instruction. It also has a rich tradition of collective action and resistance to perceived injustice. Schoolchildren challenging the established order is hardly a peculiarly French phenomenon. There is a substantial, if sometimes overlooked, British history of such action too. Pete Crockett Royal Wootton Bassett, Wiltshire Kitty Sayers is illuminating on French attitudes to protest, but she misses the mark when describing English attitudes. She says that Britons are subjects rather than citizens; that word deserves more analysis. In This Land is Our Land , Marion Shoard argues that England is in effect a colonised country, but conquered so long ago that we no longer notice how much it shapes us. Within a generation of 1066, the English landowning class had been almost entirely replaced, and many free peasants were pressed into serfdom. Shoard argues that when, centuries later, the English poor did protest, “as a defeated class, they looked only to improve the terms of their subjection, and … they failed even in that.” France, by contrast, eventually overturned its feudal order. Edward Carpenter wrote (in Towards Industrial Freedom) that victory at Waterloo had been a misfortune for England, denying us the upheaval that swept such structures away elsewhere. Perhaps that is why a French teenager reaches for the barricade and an English one reaches for a petition. The British Museum’s Bayeux tapestry exhibition is rightly presented as a marvel. As we queue to admire it, we should ask whether we still see the conquest it depicts, and its long shadow over our country, with necessary clarity. Simon Dawson Winterbourne Gunner, Wiltshire Kitty Sayers identifies the differences between the French and British education systems as a major contributory factor in why French students protest and British students don’t. Another may be in how protests are framed by the mass media in the UK. Often, the default position is what is known as the “protest paradigm”, which leads journalists to emphasise the methods used by protesters over the message; and in which even legitimate protests then receive delegitimising coverage. Changing the optics could bring more people out on to the streets, particularly if they feel they have a legitimate reason for doing so, and the media have a major role to play in creating and maintaining that environment for legitimate protest. Kevin Donnelly Sanremo, Italy Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Please email us your letter and it will be considered for publication in our letters section. https://www.newswit.com/en/ienkocrvcnzcn.text: Researcher's School of Science Arrives in Romania for Collaborative Research with World-Renowned Mathematician 5 Oct 2026 13:05 Phachara Jailoka, Ph.D., lecturer in the Department of Mathematics program, School of Science, University of Phayao, recipient of the Research Fund for Academic Staff to Conduct Research Abroad 2026, under the project " Development of optimization algorithms based on fixed point methods for enriched nonexpansive mappings," arrived at the Technical University of Cluj-Napoca, Romania, on September 30, 2026, to carry out research under this funded project. On this occasion, Phachara Jailoka Ph.D., paid a visit to and presented a souvenir to Professor Vasile Berinde, a distinguished mathematician from the Technical University of Cluj-Napoca, Romania, who is listed among the Stanford World's Top 2% Scientists and has been recognized as a Highly Cited Researcher by Thomson Reuters/Clarivate. This meeting was held to express gratitude and to mark the beginning of academic collaboration for joint research throughout the research period. This international research visit by Phachara Jailoka Ph.D., is part of the effort to promote international academic collaboration and enhance the research capabilities of academic staff at the University of Phayao in the field of advanced mathematics.
